newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal 'fever' to fuel EDP price rise.
newsitem.headline: Portugal 'fever' to fuel EDP price rise.

text.p: Shares in state-controlled utility EDP-Electricidade de Portugal looked set to soar following its privatisation on Monday but some analysts queried whether the fundamentals justified such huge enthusiasm.
Analysts widely expect the company's stock to leap in the opening days of trade as disappointed institutional investors piled into the market to buy up stock they failed to get at the privatisation.

"The shares will probably perform very well. Demand has been fantastically high and you could see the shares going up by about 30 percent during the next week," Diego Hernando, chief economist at Lisbon brokers Midas, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
The 30 percent tranche that the government sold in the electricity concern on Monday was priced at 2,250 escudos per share, the top of its pre-sale indicated range.
According to some analysts, demand could drive the stock up to between 2,700 and 3,000 escudos soon after it begins trade on Tuesday.

The state earned a little under 400 billion escudos in what was the biggest privatisation yet carried out in Portugal, with the 180 million shares sold amounting to around 25 percent of the total capitalisation of the Portuguese bourse.
"EDP is going to be the most liquid stock in the market and ...a very good vehicle for getting someone to invest in the market," said Pedro Fonseca of UBS Philips and Drew in London.
Demand from the general public outstripped supply at the privatisation 37 times.
"This will boost the liquidity of the bourse...we expect 300,000 new investors in the Portuguese market," bourse chairman Jose Carlos Pestana Teixeira told RFTV ahead of the sale.

But while agreeing that the short-term prospects of the stock were rosy, some analysts wondered whether the euphoria was not excessive given that for an initial public offering (IPO), the price was not particularly cheap.
"What we have here is a case of Portuguese fever," said one London analyst who asked not to be named. "The price (of the sale) is reasonable but it is certainly no give-away," the analyst added.

The Portuguese market has been one of the best performers in Europe over the past 18 months and Morgan Stanley, whose ratings are the international investors' Bible, recently announced it was promoting Lisbon from an emerging to developed market.

At the current level, EDP would probably lie amongst the top 25 percent of European utility companies on a price-to-cashflow basis which was a lot given that the management had little in the way of a track record, the London analyst said.
Profit last year soared 26 percent to 81 billion escudos but company remains relatively inefficient in international terms.
On one key measure of efficiency -- gigawatt hours (GWH) per man -- EDP's ratio was 1.7 against an average three in the rest of Europe and nearly six in the United States, analysts said.
Although the company has pledged to reduce its manpower by 15 percent by the end of the century, that would still leave the GWH per employee at around 2.2 or 2.3.
"It is hugely inefficient," said the London analyst.

The analyst said that the 2,250 escudo price tag put EDP on a price-earnings of 15 times expected 1997 earnings of 150 escudos per share, which was only a slight discount on Spain's Endesa, an established company with a tried and tested management, which was currently trading at around 16.6 times.

Nevertheless, the company is unlikely to come under any immediate competitive pressure over pricing, not least because the growth sector in the Portuguese market is in domestic consumption which makes it less vulnerable, analysts said.
"There is going to be a big push at the start," said the London analyst about the share price, "but one has to ask whether it will be sustainable."
($1=175 escudos)
